title: Position of adverbs 2
subtitle: Frankly, ... / we almost missed / hardly ever
summary: Choose front position for connecting, comment and viewpoint adverbs, and mid position for degree, order and indefinite frequency adverbs.

lesson.heading: What typically goes in front position
rows: connecting adverbs, which make the logical relation to the previous sentence immediately clear
The value of the yen has fallen. **As a result**, Japan faces a crisis.
time and place adverbs, which add to a time or place already mentioned
The last few days have been hot. **Tomorrow** the weather will be much cooler.
comment and viewpoint adverbs, which highlight the speaker's attitude to what they are about to say
She has just heard that her sister is ill. **Presumably**, she will want to go home.
lesson.note: Other positions are possible for all of these; front position is simply the most usual.

lesson.heading: Comment adverb or adverb of manner?

left.label: Comment adverb - front position, whole clause
left.text: It tells us the speaker's attitude to everything that follows.
examples: **Naturally**, I'll do all I can to help.
**Clearly**, he wants me to take the job.
**Plainly**, he was feeling ill at ease.

right.label: Adverb of manner - end position, modifies the verb
right.text: It tells us how the action was done.
examples: The radioactive gas occurs **naturally** in many areas.

lesson.note: Also used in both ways: curiously, frankly, honestly, oddly, seriously.

lesson.heading: Front position for special emphasis
lesson.text: Adverbs that normally sit in mid or end position can be moved to the front when we want to focus on them.

examples.text: **Regularly**, Helena works on several paintings at once.

lesson.heading: Mid position: degree adverbs
lesson.text: Degree adverbs (almost, hardly, nearly, quite, rather, scarcely) usually go in mid position. A few - completely, enormously, entirely, greatly, slightly - can also go in end position.

examples.text: The street lighting was so bad that we **almost** missed the turning.

examples.note: or I greatly admire your work.

lesson.note: Some degree adverbs avoid mid position with particular verbs: enormously is not usually used in mid position with develop, differ, go up or vary, and greatly is not normally used in mid position with care or suffer.

lesson.heading: Mid position: the order of events
lesson.text: Adverbs showing the order of events - first, last, next - usually go in mid position. They can also go at the end, but if there is a phrase giving the time of the event they come in front of it. We don't put them in front position except when listing actions.

examples.note: or I met her first in 1997.

lesson.heading: Mid position: indefinite frequency
lesson.text: One-word adverbs of indefinite frequency (hardly ever, often, rarely, regularly, seldom, and also always and never) go in mid position. But adverbial *phrases* of indefinite frequency (as a rule, on many occasions, from time to time, every so often) go in front or end position.

examples.text: We **hardly ever** see Kaspar nowadays, he's so busy at the office.
**As a rule**, I go every six months.
examples.wrong: I as a rule go every six months
examples.note: or ... every six months, as a rule.

lesson.heading: Long adverbials stay out of mid position
lesson.text: We rarely put long adverbials - clauses, prepositional phrases and noun phrases - in mid position. They go in end position, or in front position for emphasis.

examples.note: or Anxious for news, she phoned home.

examples.text: He picked up the vase **with great care**.
examples.note: or With great care he picked up the vase.
or The day before, I'd seen Tarik.

lesson.text: One word or several? A single frequency adverb (*rarely*) takes mid position; a phrase with the same meaning (*from time to time*) goes at the front or the end.

exercises.prompt: ___, I'm perfectly capable of putting up the shelf myself.
exercises.explanation: Front position, so this is a comment adverb about the whole clause.

exercises.prompt: I was brought up to earn money ___, not to steal it from others.
exercises.explanation: End position, so this is an adverb of manner: it says how the money was earned.

exercises.prompt: The chief executive has phoned me every day this week to ask whether I've made my mind up. ___, he wants me to take the job.
exercises.explanation: A comment adverb in front position: the speaker is saying how obvious the conclusion is.

exercises.prompt: I'd had very little sleep and was having difficulty thinking ___.
exercises.explanation: Here the same adverb modifies the verb, so it takes end position.

exercises.prompt: Is the adverb working as a comment adverb (about the whole clause) or as an adverb of manner (about the verb)?

items.text: Frankly, I went to sleep during his lecture - it was so boring.
She admitted frankly that she felt she wasn't doing a good job.
Plainly, he was feeling ill at ease.
She always dressed plainly at work, in a white blouse and grey skirt.
Curiously, the house has two chimneys, although there's only one fireplace.
Esther looked at him curiously, trying to work out whether he was being serious.

exercises.explanation: End position takes adverbials of definite frequency; hardly ever and always need mid position.

exercises.prompt: Carmen had ___ spoken at meetings before, so it was no surprise when she stood up.
exercises.explanation: Mid position takes one-word frequency adverbs; phrases like on many occasions go in front or end position.

exercises.prompt: It was snowing and I was ___ late for the interview.
exercises.explanation: A prepositional phrase such as by an hour can't go in mid position; the degree adverb almost can.

exercises.statement: Asthma rates in cities do not enormously differ from those in rural areas.
exercises.explanation: Asthma rates in cities do not significantly differ from those in rural areas. Enormously is not used in mid position with differ (or develop, go up, vary).

exercises.statement: Although he had to lift heavy boxes in the factory, he greatly suffered from backache.
exercises.explanation: ... he rarely suffered from backache. Greatly is not normally used in mid position with suffer (or care).

options: We seldom see Alex any more.
Seldom we see Alex any more.
We see Alex seldom any more.
exercises.explanation: Seldom is an adverb of indefinite frequency, so mid position is the one that works.

exercises.prompt: Put the long adverbial in front position for emphasis.
exercises.answer: Anxious for news, she phoned home.
alternatives: She phoned home, anxious for news.
exercises.explanation: Long adverbials go in end position, or in front position when we want to emphasise them - never in mid position.
